source.title: Efficient LLM Adversarial Training via Low-Rank Defense and Circuit-Guided Surrogates
source.authors: Weiyi He; Yu-Ping Lin; Ji-Liang Tang; Yue Xing

record.tranche_reason: The paper invokes sparse circuits as motivation and uses activation-gradient-ranked neuron pruning to build attack surrogates, but it does not test neuron interpretability, explanation accuracy, or whether neurons suffice as units for behavioral explanation.
record.gate_note: The paper reports outcomes for pruning MLP neurons and for different neuron-selection rules; these are recorded as findings about the claim's subject, but they do not measure any listed claim version. The overall LAT-ReFT comparisons combine ReFT defense with surrogate attacks, so they are not attributed to neuron pruning alone. Cited interpretability findings are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The paper prunes MLP neurons by an activation-gradient score to build a cheaper attack surrogate for latent adversarial training, and reports only attack-transfer ASR and FLOPs. It does not explain neurons, score explanations, audit neuron jobs, or build neuron-based attribution graphs. Circuit sparsity is cited as motivation only. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, but the record covers only the surrogate half. The authors conclude that LAT-ReFT, with a suffix-window ReFT defense placed away from late layers, combined with an ActGrad-pruned MLP surrogate, cuts per-step LAT FLOPs by 29.6% on average with 0.0118% trainable parameters, at a moderate robustness cost. Moderate (25%) pruning preserves attack transfer and aggressive pruning harms it. They draw no conclusions about neuron interpretability.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses ActGrad-ranked MLP-neuron pruning to speed up latent adversarial attack generation, rather than auditing or testing neuron explanations.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and pruning ratio affect transfer; at 25% pruning, the selection rule also changes ASR.

fits_no_version.finding: On IMDB/Pythia-1.4B at 25% pruning, keeping MLP neurons by activation×gradient preserves surrogate attack transfer (ASR 0.33 vs 0.26 full). Random and ActDiff selection give 0.95 and 0.97. Transfer degrades at 50–75% pruning, and EnronSpam shows a different pattern.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A minority subset of MLP neurons chosen by act×grad suffices to preserve adversarially relevant gradient directions in LLM classifiers; the outcome depends on the selection rule, the pruning ratio and the dataset.

fits_no_version.finding: ActGrad keeps more neurons in early and middle layers and prunes later layers more heavily. ActDiff spreads retention more diffusely, with more in later layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Attack-relevant MLP neurons in these classifiers concentrate in early and middle layers.

record.problems: The findings concern attack transfer in LLM-based classifiers, not explanation quality or neuron-level interpretability. The detailed pruning-ratio and selection-rule results are concentrated on Pythia-1.4B; the broader circuit-related conclusions cannot be inferred from these experiments.
record.rows_left_out: The overall LAT-ReFT robustness and efficiency comparisons in Table 1 and Tables 6 and 8 combine the defense intervention with the surrogate and do not isolate neuron pruning. The pruning heatmaps in Appendix D are not included as separate rows because the text does not report additional quantified outcomes there.

untested.parts: Qwen3-32B neuron pole audit and the one-job, two-job and not-understood shares.
Interpretability shares across other models, dense and MoE, and scale.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron, pose, and recursive generalization versus superposition.
Architecture, regularization and tools as causes of messy late-layer neurons; interpretable share rising with better tools.

Neuron-based attribution graphs explaining behaviour without a replacement model. ActGrad pruning retains attack-relevant neurons, but no attribution graph or behavioural explanation is built or evaluated.
Whether activating-example explanations predict held-out firing.
Simulation-based automated scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: The study is an adversarial-training efficiency paper. 'Circuit-guided' refers to importance-scored neuron pruning, not interpretation. The reader's T4/uses_without_test call is right; T6 would also be defensible.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B pole audit and the reported shares of one-job, two-job, and not-understood poles.
Interpretability shares across models, dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, and model scales.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose detection, and recursive generalization versus superposition.
Whether architecture, regularization, and tools explain messy neurons or change interpretability shares.
Attribution graphs explaining behavior using a large model's own neurons without a trained replacement model.
Whether explanations based on activating examples predict where neurons fire on held-out activations.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.
